findings.consequence: An admin who sends `optimized_pagination=true` with a cursor whose offset is negative, for example `0:-5:0`, gets an unhandled exception and an HTTP 500. The feature's stated purpose, reaching data beyond the normal bounds, does not work.
findings.explanation: When enable_advanced_features is on and cursor.offset < 0, get_result runs `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with start_offset set to the negative cursor.offset. The comment says Django handles negative slicing, but Django querysets do not support negative indexing and raise an AssertionError. The offset comes from the client-supplied cursor string. The audit-log endpoint turns this branch on with `optimized_pagination=true` for admins. The base-class change (`max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`) still passes a negative offset through for prev cursors.
findings.title: Negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start, which Django rejects

prs.title: Enhanced Pagination Performance for High-Volume Audit Logs

findings.consequence: An admin request to the audit log endpoint with optimized_pagination=true and a negative-offset cursor fails with an unhandled AssertionError, which returns a 500. The advertised negative-offset feature does not work. The unreachable-by-design branch also gives a misleading security and performance claim ("access to data beyond normal pagination bounds").
findings.explanation: When enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset < 0, get_result runs queryset[cursor.offset:stop]. The comment says Django handles negative slicing. It does not: QuerySet.__getitem__ asserts that negative indexing is not supported. The audit log endpoint passes enable_advanced_features=True whenever optimized_pagination=true and the user is a superuser or has global access. A client-supplied cursor with a negative offset, such as "0:-5:1", therefore reaches this branch. The change also adds no validation that rejects such offsets. If it did slice, the result would be wrong anyway, because the stop bound would be the sum of a negative start and the limit.
findings.title: Negative-offset path slices the queryset with a negative start, which Django rejects

findings.consequence: Traces with very deep span parent chains (more than about 1000 levels) can be flushed as several fragmented segments. This is a rare case.
findings.explanation: The loop bound in add-buffer.lua went from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`. The old comment said the limit meant segment trees deeper than 10k might not join correctly. With 1000, a parent chain of more than about 1000 redirects ends the loop before reaching the real root set. `set_span_id` is then an intermediate span, and the span is merged into the wrong set key. The segment is split, so later spans can land in a different set from the rest of the segment.
findings.title: Redirect-chain traversal limit cut from 10000 to 1000

prs.title: Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert

findings.consequence: API clients, dashboards and alerts that read `count` from events-stats for allowlisted projects can get undercounted or differently scaled values with no signal in the response. A sample_weight column missing from the errors dataset would make the query fail instead.
findings.explanation: _get_event_stats now calls is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects. When every project is in the allowlist and the dataset is errors, or discover with "event.type:error" in the query, it rewrites "count()" to "upsampled_count() as count". That function compiles to toInt64(sum(sample_weight)). Nothing in the repo defines or populates a sample_weight column; the only matches are in this feature's own code. Events that lack the weight (NULL or 0) are not counted by sum(sample_weight), so the same request returns a different `count` series than before. The request has no opt-in or opt-out flag. The same column rewrite is applied to the topEvents path. The eligibility result is also cached for 60 seconds under a key that ignores allowlist changes, and invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called anywhere. After an allowlist change, a project can keep returning the old kind of count for u…
findings.title: events-stats silently rewrites count() to sum(sample_weight) for allowlisted projects, which can change the response values

findings.consequence: For up to a minute after an allowlist change, counts can be wrong. Projects removed from the allowlist can get null or zero counts from sum(sample_weight), and added projects keep unupsampled counts.
findings.explanation: is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects caches the allowlist result under a key built from the org id and project ids, for 60 seconds. invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but nothing in src calls it. The grep found no callers, and the option is changed only via the options system. The docstring says to call it when the allowlist changes, but that never happens. The helper's own NOTE says the allowlist is read fresh each time, which contradicts the cache. Example: a project is added to or removed from the allowlist. For up to 60s, queries still use the old eligibility. A newly removed project would then run upsampled_count() (sum(sample_weight)) on events that lack sample_weight. A newly added project would keep returning unupsampled counts.
findings.title: Allowlist eligibility cached for 60s with no invalidation caller

prs.title: feat(upsampling) - Support upsampled error count with performance optimizations

findings.consequence: A regression in handling a missing GitHub installation would go undetected, because the test passes for an unrelated reason.
findings.explanation: The test never visits init_path, so no pipeline is started. It then sends the OAuth callback with an arbitrary state ("ddd023d8..."), which cannot match any pipeline signature. The response is the generic "Invalid installation request." (integration.py:132), produced by the missing or invalid pipeline or the state mismatch. The 404 stub for /app/installations/{id}, which raises "The GitHub installation could not be found." in build_integration (integration.py:356), is never reached. The old assertion for that message was replaced with the generic one, so the test would pass whether or not the 404 handling works.
findings.title: test_installation_not_found no longer verifies the installation-not-found path

prs.title: GitHub OAuth Security Enhancement

findings.consequence: After a hang, the stuck flusher process keeps running and a duplicate is spawned for the same shards. Repeated hangs accumulate leaked processes, and two flushers can flush and produce the same segments concurrently. On shutdown, spawned processes are not terminated.
findings.explanation: The old code called self.process.kill() unconditionally. The new code only calls kill() when `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The processes are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. That class derives from `BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.context.Process` (what `multiprocessing.Process` refers to). The isinstance check is therefore False for every real production process. When a process is detected as "hang" (alive but not updating healthy_since), kill() is skipped, and `_create_process_for_shards` starts a second process for the same shards while the hung one stays alive. The same check is used in join() before process.terminate() (line 346), so real processes are not terminated there either.
findings.title: Hung flusher processes are never killed: isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process fails for SpawnProcess

findings.consequence: The intended synchronization after advancing drift does not happen. If the flusher has not flushed by the time `step.join()` runs, `(msg,) = messages` can fail intermittently. The added line gives false confidence.
findings.explanation: test_basic patches "time.sleep" to `lambda _: None` at its start. The new `time.sleep(0.1)` calls the attribute on the time module, so it hits the patched lambda and returns immediately. The comment says it gives the flusher time to process after the drift change, but it waits for nothing. The test still depends on `step.join()` and its own timing to collect the flushed message.
findings.title: Added time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

prs.title: Span Buffer Multiprocess Enhancement with Health Monitoring

findings.consequence: The `queued` value in AssignmentSource, and in the dict passed to the sync_assignee_outbound task, is stale and identical across all instances. Any code that uses it for ordering, de-duplication or staleness checks will get wrong results.
findings.explanation: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls `timezone.now()` once, when the class body runs at module import. Every AssignmentSource built through `from_integration` gets that same frozen timestamp, which is the process start time and not the time the assignment was queued. A `dataclasses.field(default_factory=timezone.now)` default would give each instance its own timestamp.
findings.title: AssignmentSource.queued default is evaluated once at import time

findings.consequence: Every incident occurrence's monitor context shows the raw numeric schedule_type, not the label the code meant to show.
findings.explanation: get_monitor_environment_context copies the monitor config and replaces schedule_type with its display string. The returned dict then uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the local `config`, so the copy is dead code. The event context therefore carries the raw schedule_type value rather than the human-readable one.

findings.consequence: process_detectors raises TypeError for any detector of type metric_alert_fire, so the whole detector-processing run fails instead of skipping or no-oping.
findings.explanation: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler with an empty body (`pass`). StatefulDetectorHandler declares abstract methods (get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data), and the subclass implements none of them. MetricAlertFire sets `detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler` (grouptype.py:27). Detector.detector_handler then calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)` (models/detector.py:86), which raises TypeError ("Can't instantiate abstract class"). The old class had a working evaluate() returning [].

findings.consequence: If the calendar service constructor or deleteEvent fails during reschedule or cancel, the error is not logged by the catch block. It surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection, which can crash the Node process or leave the old calendar event in place without any trace.
findings.explanation: The change made the forEach callback async in vital/lib/reschedule.ts and wipemycalother/lib/reschedule.ts, and added `await getCalendar(...)` inside it. The surrounding try/catch used to catch a synchronous throw from getCalendar. forEach ignores the promise the async callback returns, so a rejection from getCalendar (for example a failed dynamic import in appStore) or from deleteEvent is no longer caught. The same pattern is in bookings.tsx around lines 553-566, which has no try/catch at all. The reschedule flow also does not wait for the calendar deletions, so it can continue or return before they finish. I checked every other getCalendar caller (EventManager, handleCancelBooking, handleNewBooking, CalendarManager, videoClient and the payment code). They all await the result correctly.
findings.title: Async forEach callback escapes try/catch, so getCalendar/deleteEvent failures become unhandled rejections

prs.title: Async import of the appStore packages

findings.consequence: The TypeScript build or type-check fails while that component exists. Any code path that uses the security modal can't compile cleanly.
findings.explanation: The change made `backupCode` a required parameter of `TwoFactorAuthAPI.disable(password, code, backupCode)`. `apps/web/components/security/DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx:38` still calls `TwoFactorAuthAPI.disable(password, totpCode)` with two arguments. Only `settings/DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx` was updated. The old caller now fails type-checking because the argument is missing. If it is run anyway, `backupCode` is `undefined`, and `JSON.stringify` drops it from the request body.
findings.title: TwoFactorAuthAPI.disable now requires a third argument that an existing caller does not pass

findings.consequence: A backup code that is meant to be single-use can be replayed in parallel requests to create several sessions. A used code can also be restored by a concurrent write. The attacker needs the password, because the password check runs when no `totpCode` is given. The weakness is therefore limited to defeating the single-use guarantee of the second factor.
findings.explanation: The backup code branch reads and decrypts `user.backupCodes` in the initial `findUnique`. It checks the submitted code with `indexOf`, sets that slot to null in memory, and then runs an unconditional `prisma.user.update` that overwrites the whole encrypted blob. The update has no compare-and-swap condition, such as a check that the stored value is unchanged, and no transaction or lock. Two concurrent logins with the same valid backup code both read the blob while the code is still present. Both pass the `indexOf` check, both write back, and both `authorize` calls succeed. A concurrent login with a different code can also overwrite the first request's write, which restores the first code. That code can then be used again. I checked the other points in the hypothesis and they don't hold. `checkRateLimitAndThrowError` runs after the user lookup but before the backup code branch, so guesses…
findings.title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so one code can be used more than once

findings.consequence: An unauthenticated caller who knows only an email address can obtain a session for any account without 2FA, including Google/SAML-provider accounts. For 2FA accounts, a leaked backup code is enough, with no password needed. This is full account takeover.
findings.explanation: In authorize, the provider check (line 113), the missing-password check (line 117) and the password verification (line 121) are all guarded by `!credentials.totpCode`. Nothing later verifies the password independently. For a user with twoFactorEnabled=false, a request with only email and any non-empty totpCode skips every credential check. The `else if (user.twoFactorEnabled)` branch (line 157) is not entered, so the function reaches `return` at line 205 and returns the user. This also works for non-CAL identity-provider users and users with no password. The new backup-code branch (line 131) has the same flaw. For a 2FA-enabled user, a valid backup code plus any dummy totpCode logs in without the password, because the password check at line 121 was skipped and the totp branch is never reached.
findings.title: Password check skipped whenever totpCode is supplied; authentication bypass

prs.title: feat: 2fa backup codes

findings.consequence: When a caller omits `externalCalendarId`, a Google event stored in a non-primary destination calendar is not updated or deleted in the right calendar. `updateEvent` sends `calendarId: undefined` and fails. `deleteEvent` targets the primary calendar, so the event is left behind or the delete returns an error. This is a regression from the previous fallback to the destination calendar's externalId.
findings.explanation: The old fallback was `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId`. The change replaced it with `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId`. That fallback only runs when `externalCalendarId` is falsy, so the predicate compares each `cal.externalId` to a falsy value. It effectively never matches and always yields undefined. In `updateEvent`, `calendarId` is then undefined. In `deleteEvent`, it falls through to "primary".
findings.title: Google updateEvent/deleteEvent fallback to destinationCalendar can never match

findings.consequence: A booking with a Google Meet location and no destination calendar crashes in EventManager.create with 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading integration)'. The intended fallback to Cal Video never runs, and booking creation or confirmation fails.
findings.explanation: The change makes destinationCalendar an array. The Meet fallback now reads `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` and then `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration`. When the array is empty, the destructured value is undefined and the property access throws a TypeError. The updated callers (bookingReminder, confirm.handler, editLocation.handler) now pass `[]` when neither the booking nor the user has a destination calendar. The old code used `evt.destinationCalendar?.integration`, which was safe in that case. The handlers' empty-array fallbacks were not checked for a path that reaches `create` with an empty array.
findings.title: EventManager.create throws when location is Google Meet and destinationCalendar is empty

findings.consequence: For that collective event, no calendar event is created on the other hosts' destination calendars. The booking is also saved with no destinationCalendar connection (line 1874).
findings.explanation: evt.destinationCalendar is null when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar (lines 1063-1067). The collective-event step at 1077-1079 then calls `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`. Optional chaining on null does nothing, so the calendars collected from the other hosts at lines 991-994 are discarded. Example: a COLLECTIVE event where the organizer has no destination calendar and the other hosts do.
findings.title: Collective team members' destination calendars dropped when organizer has none

findings.consequence: With billing enabled, the organization is created with its slug claimed immediately, before payment or verification. The pending-slug flow that uses `requestedSlug` is bypassed. With billing disabled (self-hosted), the organization is created with no slug and no requestedSlug, so it is unreachable by slug.
findings.explanation: The change rewrote `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` as `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`. This drops the negation, so the condition is flipped and not just reformatted. The old code set `slug` only when billing was disabled, and set `metadata.requestedSlug` only when billing was enabled. The new code sets `slug` when billing is enabled, and sets `requestedSlug` in that same case. When billing is disabled, no slug is set at all, and `requestedSlug` is not set either. This change has nothing to do with the destinationCalendar array refactor in the rest of the PR.
findings.title: Organization slug condition inverted on IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED

findings.consequence: Cancelled or rescheduled bookings can still send workflow reminders, or leave orphaned reminder rows, when the process stops before the unawaited promises finish. Failures are silent.
findings.explanation: The old handler awaited the workflowReminder deleteMany calls inside Promise.all. The new code calls the async deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder without await or collecting their promises (handleCancelBooking.ts 485-491). The handler therefore returns after sendCancelledEmails without waiting for the Twilio cancel or the DB delete/update. Errors are swallowed inside those helpers with console.log. In a serverless runtime the response can end before the work finishes, which leaves SMS reminders scheduled at Twilio or reminder rows not updated, so a cancelled booking can still send reminders. The same pattern is in handleNewBooking.ts 964-976 for reschedules. The try/catch there cannot catch rejections from unawaited async calls, so it is ineffective. For reschedules, the email path with immediateDelete=true only cancels at SendGrid. It neither deletes nor marks…
findings.title: Reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget and no longer part of the awaited cancel flow

findings.consequence: One bad reminder blocks cancellation cleanup for all the others. Cancelled rows pile up and get re-sent to SendGrid on every run. The only trace is a console.log.
findings.explanation: The loop awaits client.request for each reminder inside a single try. The Prisma delete calls are lazy and only run when awaited, and they are only awaited in Promise.all after the loop. If any request throws, for example on a SendGrid error, a rate limit or a null referenceId, control jumps to the catch. The remaining reminders are never cancelled. The deletes already queued for earlier reminders never execute either, even though their SendGrid sends were cancelled. Those rows stay cancelled:true and are retried on every cron run.
findings.title: One failed SendGrid cancel aborts the whole loop and no reminder rows are deleted

findings.consequence: Reminders marked `cancelled` for cancelled or rescheduled bookings, or edited workflows, are never cancelled at SendGrid. The attendee still receives the emails for those bookings. The `cancelled` rows stay in the DB and the cron retries and fails on every run.
findings.explanation: The new cancel loop in scheduleEmailReminders.ts calls `client.request` from `@sendgrid/client`. The file only calls `sgMail.setApiKey`, which configures the mail service's own client. It never calls `client.setApiKey`. In the code I could see, the only `client.setApiKey` is inside emailReminderManager.ts (line 26), which this cron file doesn't import. The first `client.request` for a cancelled reminder therefore fails with an auth error. The surrounding try/catch swallows the error and only logs it. This also aborts the whole loop, so no later reminder is processed. No cancelled reminder is deleted from the DB or cancelled at SendGrid.
findings.title: Cron cancel loop uses SendGrid client without an API key

findings.consequence: A single cancelled SMS reminder can stop cancellation of every email reminder. This email cron also deletes SMS rows or hits SendGrid with invalid batch ids.
findings.explanation: The findMany for cancelled reminders filters only on cancelled and scheduledDate, with no method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL. Cancelled SMS reminders therefore match, and they may have a null or non-SendGrid referenceId. Sending batch_id null to SendGrid is likely to fail, and a failure aborts the whole loop (see the main finding).
findings.title: Cancelled-reminder query has no method filter, so non-email reminders are sent to SendGrid

prs.title: Comprehensive workflow reminder management for booking lifecycle events

findings.consequence: Valid slots are wrongly removed for any host with more than one working-hours range on a day. Slots that start in range but end after closing time are still offered. Both give wrong booking availability.
findings.explanation: In the new working-hours block, `end` is computed from `slotStartTime` (the same expression as `start`) instead of `slotEndTime`. The slot's end is therefore never checked against `workingHour.endTime`, and a slot that starts inside the hours but runs past closing is not caught. The `find` callback also returns true, meaning 'unavailable', as soon as any entry for that weekday fails the bounds test. A user with split hours on one day, such as 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00, has two entries for that day. A 14:00 slot fails the first entry (start 840 is not below 540, but end 840 is above 720), so `find` returns true and the slot is rejected, even though the second entry contains it. The same happens with multiple schedule entries on a day, or after aggregation.
findings.title: Working-hours check in checkIfIsAvailable compares the slot start twice and rejects slots that fit another working-hours entry

findings.consequence: A zero-length date override (start equals end) does not block the day in this check. It relies on the other branches, which treat only slots at or before the start as outside the override.
findings.explanation: `dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two distinct objects, so it is always false. The zero-length override case, which is meant to mark the day unavailable, is never handled by this branch.
findings.title: Object identity comparison of dayjs instances is always false

prs.title: Advanced date override handling and timezone compatibility improvements

findings.consequence: On a misconfigured deployment, an unauthenticated caller can create or overwrite any user's app credentials through this endpoint. That includes replacing OAuth tokens for any user.
findings.explanation: The handler compares `req.headers[name] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` with no check that the secret is configured. If APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is true but CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset, a request with no secret header has `undefined` on both sides. The `!==` is then false and the request is treated as authenticated. The comparison is also not constant-time. The handler goes on to write arbitrary `key` JSON into the credential of any userId, and the decryption key falls back to an empty string.
findings.title: Webhook secret check passes when the secret env var is unset and the header is missing

findings.consequence: Timing-based recovery of the shared secret is theoretically possible and would let an attacker overwrite any user's app credentials. Malformed requests produce 500 responses and server error noise rather than clean 4xx responses.
findings.explanation: The unset-secret bypass does not happen. APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED (packages/lib/constants.ts:103) is truthy only when both CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET and CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY are set, and the handler returns 403 before the secret check otherwise. So `undefined === undefined` and the empty-string decrypt key cannot be reached. Two weaker defects remain. (1) The secret is compared with `!==` at lines 23-26, which is not constant-time, so a remote caller could in principle recover it through timing. If the header is sent twice, Node gives an array, which never equals the secret; that case is safe. (2) `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` at line 29 is not caught. Neither are `JSON.parse` or `symmetricDecrypt` at lines 56-58. A malformed body, or keys that fail to decrypt, throws an unhandled error and the caller gets a 500 instead of a 400.
findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==`; invalid bodies are not handled

findings.consequence: In credential-sync mode, refreshing a token overwrites the stored refresh_token with the string "refresh_token". It also stores a NaN expiry_date. The next refresh then fails and the integration breaks until the user reconnects.
findings.explanation: z.string().toString() and z.string().optional().toString() both return "[object Object]", because Zod schemas don't override toString. The two computed keys are therefore the same, and the second (z.unknown().optional()) overwrites the first (z.number()). The schema is effectively {access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown optional}. z.object strips unknown keys by default. In credential-sync mode, a payload like {access_token, refresh_token, expires_in} parses successfully, but the returned data holds only access_token. The expires_in and refresh_token fields are dropped, and the intended "any number property is the expiry" rule is never enforced. The code at line 26 then sees no refresh_token and writes the literal placeholder "refresh_token". Callers such as zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts:119-124 copy newTokens.refresh_token into the stored key, and compute newTokens.expires…
findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema collapses to one "[object Object]" key and strips real token fields

findings.consequence: The stored credential's real refresh token is replaced by the bogus string. Any later refresh that does not go through the sync endpoint fails with invalid_grant.
findings.explanation: When the response has no refresh_token, the parser sets it to the literal string "refresh_token". Callers such as Office365 calendar merge `tokenResponse.data` into the stored credential.
findings.title: Placeholder refresh_token written over missing refresh token

findings.consequence: With sharing enabled, token refresh fails for axios-based and SDK-based apps. In hubspot it can overwrite the stored credential with a corrupt value. Anyone who can reach the sync endpoint can request tokens for a given user id and app slug, because the request carries no authentication.
findings.explanation: When credential sharing is enabled, the helper returns the raw fetch Response. It sends no auth header or secret, and it never checks response.ok. The non-sync branch returns whatever the refresh callback returns, which is an axios response in zohocrm and bigin and a parsed token object from the SDK in hubspot. zohocrm reads `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error`, and a fetch Response has no `.data`, so that line throws a TypeError. hubspot assigns the result to `HubspotToken` and reads `.expiresIn` and `.accessToken`, which are undefined on a Response. It then writes that Response to the credential key. Error statuses (401/500) are never detected.
findings.title: Sync branch returns raw fetch Response, unauthenticated and unchecked, breaking callers

findings.consequence: Constructing the Salesforce calendar service fails on every call, so the Salesforce integration breaks. Even with the import added, the connection would still use the stale access token.
findings.explanation: The change adds `await prisma.credential.update(...)` in SalesforceCalendarService.getClient, but the file has no `prisma` import (the only occurrence of `prisma` in the file is that call). This throws a ReferenceError (or fails type-checking) after every successful token refresh. In addition, the returned jsforce.Connection is built with the old `credentialKey.access_token`, not the newly refreshed `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`.
findings.title: Salesforce getClient uses prisma without importing it; also ignores refreshed token

prs.title: OAuth credential sync and app integration enhancements

findings.consequence: Reminders that can never be sent are reselected and reprocessed on every cron run until their scheduled date passes. This adds repeated DB work, and the new retry cap does not cover these cases.
findings.explanation: retryCount is incremented only on a thrown error or a falsy scheduleSMS result. Both of those are inside the `if (message?.length && sendTo)` block, and that block has no else branch. If the message is empty, or sendTo is null (for example, no smsReminderNumber on the booking), nothing is updated. The row stays scheduled=false with retryCount=0. It matches the findMany query on every cron run, and the new `retryCount > 1` cleanup can never remove it. The existing deleteMany on past scheduledDate eventually removes it, so the reprocessing is bounded by the reminder's scheduledDate. It is not infinite.
findings.title: Reminders with empty message or missing sendTo never get retryCount incremented

findings.consequence: One failing retry-count write stops the batch. Later SMS reminders are not scheduled until the next cron run, and the cron call gets an error response instead of "SMS scheduled".
findings.explanation: The new `prisma.workflowReminder.update` in the catch block (lines 190-197) is not wrapped in its own try/catch. If it throws (DB error, or the row was deleted concurrently, which gives P2025 record-not-found), the exception escapes the for-loop and the handler. The remaining reminders in `unscheduledReminders` are then not processed, and the cron call returns an error. The same applies to the new else-branch update at lines 178-186, which sits inside the try, so its failure triggers a second update in the catch. The migration and schema change itself is compatible: it adds a NOT NULL column with DEFAULT 0, so existing rows are fine. The unscoped `retryCount > 1` delete clause is harmless today because only this handler increments retryCount.
findings.title: Retry-count update inside catch is unguarded and can abort the whole batch

findings.consequence: Email or other-method reminder rows with retryCount above 1 are deleted by the SMS cron. Their retries stop, and any provider-scheduled sends can no longer be tracked or cancelled through the row.
findings.explanation: The new second OR branch of deleteMany is `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` and has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter. The first branch is scoped to SMS. The second branch matches any WorkflowReminder row, including email and WhatsApp reminders, whenever retryCount is above 1.
findings.title: retryCount cleanup clause deletes reminders of every method

findings.consequence: A blacklisted address still receives a notification email. Existing attendees get redundant mails. Mixed-case addresses evade the blacklist and the duplicate check, so they are stored as duplicate or blocked attendees.
findings.explanation: The handler filters `guests` into `uniqueGuests`. It drops existing attendees and blacklisted addresses, and only `uniqueGuests` is saved through `createMany`. The final call is `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)`, which passes the original unfiltered `guests`. If the input has an address from `BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` or one that is already an attendee, the email still goes to it. The blacklist check therefore does not stop the email, and existing attendees get a duplicate 'guests added' mail. Separately, the blacklist entries are lowercased but `guest` is not. The blacklist check and the attendee de-duplication are both case-sensitive, so `Blocked@x.com` passes the filter and is saved as a new attendee.
findings.title: Notification emails sent to the raw guest list, not the filtered list that was saved

findings.consequence: Team admins who are not owners are wrongly rejected with FORBIDDEN when adding guests to team bookings.
findings.explanation: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`. It should be true if the user is either. A team admin who is not the owner fails this check. Such a user can only add guests if they are also the organizer or an attendee. The fallback `teamId ?? 0` also queries team 0 for bookings with no team.
findings.title: Team admin/owner check uses && instead of ||

findings.consequence: The anonymous device_limit is not enforced. Any client that retries a rejected request is let in without being counted, so the limit can be exceeded without bound.
findings.explanation: Authenticate now rejects a request only when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. In impl.go, tagDeviceUI (lines 83-95) calls localCache.SetDefault(key) before CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the key is already cached. The cache TTL is 29 minutes, and every later request from that device ID hits `localCache.Get(key)` and returns nil. Authenticate then treats the tag as successful and grants anonymous access. So a new device over the limit is rejected once, then admitted on its next request, and stays admitted for up to 29 minutes. Any other error from CreateOrUpdateDevice leaves the key cached in the same way.
findings.title: Device limit is bypassed on the second request because the rejected device stays in the local cache

prs.title: Anonymous: Add configurable device limit

findings.consequence: If a user is denied on one resource, a different resource whose name and parent concatenate to the same string is wrongly denied for the cache TTL. This is a false denial, not a bypass. It is hard to debug and is limited to colliding UIDs that contain underscores.
findings.explanation: userPermDenialCacheKey joins userUID, action, name and parent with '_', and none of the fields are escaped. Name and parent are request-supplied, and Grafana UIDs can contain underscores. Name "a_b" with parent "c" and name "a" with parent "b_c" both produce the key "<ns>.perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c". Check() reads this key from permDenialCache and returns Allowed=false immediately, before any permission lookup. The key also leaves out the identity type. I only inspected the key-building code and the Check() lookup, not the callers or cacheWrap.
findings.title: Denial cache key is built with an ambiguous '_' separator, so different resources can share a cached denial

findings.consequence: Users see edit and delete actions on federated rule groups that were previously blocked. Those actions are not meant to be allowed, so the UI exposes them and the backend rejects them.
findings.explanation: The old useAllAlertRuleAbilities computed isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group), which made federated Mimir rules immutable. The change makes it delegate to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes isFederated = false (TODO). The isFederatedRuleGroup import was also removed. For a CombinedRule in a federated group, immutableRule is now false. Update, Delete, Pause, Restore and DeletePermanently therefore report as supported, if the user has the permissions.
findings.title: Federated rule group guard dropped from useAllAlertRuleAbilities

findings.consequence: Users with edit and export permission cannot pause, export, restore or permanently delete Grafana-managed recording rules from the rule list menu. This regresses behavior that worked before the list stopped calling the ruler API.
findings.explanation: The ruler-based abilities gate ModifyExport, Pause, Restore and DeletePermanently on rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule), which is true for both alerting and recording Grafana rules. The new useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities gates the same actions on prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule), which is false for recording rules. The rule list now uses the prom-based path, and AlertRuleMenu ORs it with the ruler path. A Grafana recording rule shown in the list gets no pause or export entries, although it did in the ruler-based menu. No security bypass was found. The permission checks still use folder permissions, and the new path only narrows access.
findings.title: Pause/Export/Restore/DeletePermanently disabled for Grafana recording rules in prom-based abilities

findings.consequence: When the filtered results are re-ordered, filtered or extended, Grafana rule items are matched by position. Per-item state, such as the action buttons' modals and silence drawer, can be attached to the wrong rule. The console also logs a key warning.
findings.explanation: The change replaced GrafanaRuleLoader with GrafanaRuleListItem and dropped the `key={key}` prop. The element is returned from `rules.map(...)` inside the `<ul>`. The sibling `datasource` and default branches still pass `key`. Without a key, React falls back to index-based reconciliation and logs a missing-key warning.
findings.title: Missing React key on GrafanaRuleListItem in filtered rule list

findings.consequence: In mode 3 the legacy store silently misses creates, updates and deletes, so it drifts from unified storage. The failures show up only as legacy error metrics.
findings.explanation: In Create (line 51), Update (line 135), Delete (line 110) and DeleteCollection (line 163), the background goroutine derives its timeout context from the request `ctx`. That context is cancelled once the REST handler returns, and each method returns right after starting the goroutine. The legacy write is therefore usually cancelled before it completes, or fails with context canceled. The 10s timeout never applies as intended. The goroutines should use a context detached from request cancellation, such as `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`.
findings.title: Async legacy writes use the request context, so they are cancelled when the handler returns

findings.consequence: Storage errors are reported as legacy errors, and legacy DeleteCollection results are mixed into the storage metrics. This misleads dashboards used during a migration.
findings.explanation: On a storage failure, Create (line 45) and Update (line 129) call recordLegacyDuration, although the call being timed was the Storage call. In the DeleteCollection goroutine (line 166), the legacy call's duration and error are recorded with recordStorageDuration.
findings.title: Storage and legacy durations are recorded under the wrong metric

findings.consequence: Metric label cardinality is unbounded, and delete metrics are not grouped by kind. Downstream logs lose the name, kind and method values.
findings.explanation: At line 106 the success path calls recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, ...), passing `name` where every other call passes options.Kind. This creates a metric label value for each deleted object name. Line 97 also builds the context logger from `d.Log` instead of the enriched `log`.
findings.title: Delete records storage duration with the object name as the kind label

findings.consequence: Normal, successful cleanup runs flood the logs with Error entries carrying thousands of IDs. This hides real errors and can trigger error-level alerting. The cost is high log volume and wasted memory and I/O.
findings.explanation: The new batched cleanup logs two Error-level lines per batch: "Tags to clean" and "cleaned tags". CleanAnnotations does the same for the by-time and by-count passes. Each line includes the full `ids` slice, the SQL condition and `err`, which is nil on those paths. These look like leftover debug statements. Every batch emits them, including the final empty batch. Batches can hold up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize IDs, and the loop runs until nothing is left to delete. A large backlog therefore produces very large error-level log output.
findings.title: Debug logging at Error level dumps full ID lists on every cleanup batch

findings.consequence: Cleanup jobs run ten times more often on every instance, adding database load. With long-running cleanups this also makes overlapping runs more likely.
findings.explanation: `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` became `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` in CleanUpService.Run. The change is unrelated to the annotation batching and looks like a debugging leftover. Each clean() run has a 9-minute timeout, so runs now trigger ten times more often than before. Every run does all the cleanup jobs, including the annotation cleanup, which now issues extra queries.
findings.title: Cleanup ticker interval cut from 10 minutes to 1 minute

findings.consequence: A user who turns on the sqlExpressions feature flag still cannot create SQL expressions, because every SQL query is rejected at parse time. The `NewSQLCommand` path in ReadQuery is unreachable. If the stub is meant to disable the feature, the dead flag check hides that. If it is meant to honour the flag, the logic is broken.
findings.explanation: enableSqlExpressions sets `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)`, so the variable holds the negation of the flag. It then returns false when that negation is true. The fall-through path also returns false. Every path returns false, whatever the flag value. The `QueryTypeSQL` case in ReadQuery therefore always returns "sqlExpressions is not implemented", even when the feature flag is on. The flag check does nothing, and the inverted variable name suggests a logic error.
findings.title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false and inverts the feature flag
